chapterTag.category: AP Calc BC BC-4 — Polar Coordinates

body.en: Polar coordinates locate points by radius and angle, and turn area into a sweep of the radius about the origin.
The polar curve \( r=\sin(k\theta) \) traces a rose. Change \( k \) and count the petals — odd \( k \) gives \( k \) petals, even \( k \) gives \( 2k \).

ariaLabel.en: The polar rose curve r equals sine of k theta

caption.en: Sampled points around the rose, one per petal-cycle interval

note.en: Polar area is \( \tfrac12\displaystyle\int r^{2}\,d\theta \) — one of the headline BC integrals.

body.en: Convert with \( x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta \). The area swept is \( A=\tfrac12\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta r^{2}\,d\theta \). Slope follows from treating \( x \) and \( y \) as parametric in \( \theta \).

caption.en: Polar area is generated as the radial arm \( r(\theta) \) sweeps through angle \( d\theta \), creating an infinitesimal circular sector with area \( dA = \frac{1}{2} r^2\,d\theta \). Integrating across \( [\alpha, \beta] \) yields the total enclosed area \( A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta \).

label.en: ⚠️ AP Exam Traps: Polar Coordinates & Calculus

body.en:
• The Missing \( \frac{1}{2} \) Factor: The single most frequent student error in polar integration is omitting the \( \frac{1}{2} \) factor. Always write \( A = \frac{1}{2} \int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta \).
  • Area Between Two Polar Curves: If region \( R \) lies between outer curve \( r_1(\theta) \) and inner curve \( r_2(\theta) \), the area is \( \frac{1}{2} \int [r_1^2 - r_2^2]\,d\theta \). It is NEVER \( \frac{1}{2}\int [r_1 - r_2]^2\,d\theta \)!
  • Polar Slope \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) vs. \( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \): The derivative \( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \) measures how fast the radius grows with respect to angle — it is NOT the slope of the tangent line. To find slope, apply the product rule to \( y = r\sin\theta \) and \( x = r\cos\theta \): \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}. \]
  • Petal Bounds: To find integration limits for a single petal, find consecutive angles where \( r(\theta) = 0 \). For \( r = \sin(2\theta) \), \( 2\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 0 \) and \( 2\theta = \pi \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/2 \), so the petal spans \( [0, \pi/2] \).
Find the area enclosed by \( r=2 \). \[ \tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}2^{2}\,d\theta=\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot2\pi=4\pi. \]

Find the area enclosed by one petal of \(r=\sin(2\theta)\).

One petal: \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2\).

\[A=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2(2\theta)\,d\theta=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1-\cos(4\theta)}{2}\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{8}.\]

question.en: Convert the polar equation \(r=4\cos\theta\) to rectangular form and identify the curve.

solution.en: Multiply both sides by \(r\): \(r^2=4r\cos\theta\Rightarrow x^2+y^2=4x\Rightarrow(x-2)^2+y^2=4\). Circle, centre \((2,0)\), radius \(2\).

question.en: Find the slope of the line tangent to the cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\) at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

solution.en: Write rectangular coordinates in terms of \(\theta\): \(x = (1+\cos\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta + \cos^2\theta\), and \(y = (1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta = \sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta\). Differentiate: \(\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta - 2\cos\theta\sin\theta\); at \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -1 - 0 = -1\). Next, \(\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \cos\theta + \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\); at \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0 + 0 - 1 = -1\). Thus, the tangent slope is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{-1} = 1\).
